title: Definition
body_md:
Given positive integers $w$ and $h$, the \emph{ordered configuration space of $n$ open unit-squares in the $w$ by $h$ rectangle} $R_{w,h}$ is the space of embeddings of $n$ labeled squares in the Euclidean rectangle $R_{w,h}$ such that the sides of the squares are parallel to the sides of the rectangle.
We write \emph{$SF_{n}(R_{w,h})$} for this configuration space.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The quotient of $SF_{n}(R_{w,h})$ by the $S_{n}$-action is $SC_{n}(R_{w,h})$, the \emph{unordered configuration space of $n$ open unit-squares in $R_{w,h}$}.
The fundamental group of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h})$ is the \emph{square-section braid group $SBr_{n}(R_{w,h})$}.

label: rightmost config space unordered
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{rightmost config space unordered}
Given a $k$-tuple $\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dots, \lambda_{k})$ of non-negative integers, let $|\lambda|:=\lambda_{1}+\cdots+\lambda_{k}$.
We write $SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h})$ for the \emph{partially ordered configuration space of $|\lambda|$ open unit-squares in the $w$ by $h$ rectangle $R_{w,h}$ such that $\lambda_{j}$ squares are labeled $j$}.
We write \emph{$SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{l};\lambda_{l+1};\dots; \lambda_{k})$} for the subspace of $SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h})$ consisting of configurations in which the only squares that are to the right, i.e., have larger $x$-coordinates, of a square labeled $j\ge l$ are those labeled $i$ where $i>j$.
If $l=2$, we write $SC_{|\lambda|}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{l};\lambda_{l+1};\dots; \lambda_{k})$ for $SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{l};\lambda_{l+1};\dots; \lambda_{k})$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: In $SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{l};\dots; \lambda_{k})$ all squares labeled a fixed $i\ge l$ are aligned horizontally (in a column), and the squares labeled $j<l$ can be anywhere as long as they do not pass to the right of any square with label at least $l$.

label: arc complex defn
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{arc complex defn}
Given $\lambda=(\lambda_{1},\dots, \lambda_{k})$ and $\lambda'=(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2}, 0, \lambda_{3},\dots, \lambda_{k})$, let
\[
MV_{m}\big(SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})\big):=SC_{|\lambda|}(R_{w,h}; m+1; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k}).
\]
Letting $m$ vary, the $MV_{m}\big(SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})\big)$ come together to form an augmented semisimplicial space $MV_{\bullet}\big(SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})\big)$.
Ordering the $m+1$
squares labeled $2$ from top to bottom, the $l$-th face map 
\[
d_{l}:MV_{m}\big(SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})\big)\to MV_{m-1}\big(SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})\big)
\]
changes the label of the $l$-th square labeled $2$ to $1$.
Additionally, as $MV_{-1}\big(SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})\big)=SC_{\lambda'}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})\simeq SC_{|\lambda'|}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})$, there is an augmentation map
\[
\Big\|MV_{\bullet}\big(SC_{\lambda}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})\big)\Big\|\to SC_{|\lambda'|}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k}).
\]
We call this complex the \emph{right Mayer--Vietoris complex of $SC_{|\lambda'|}(R_{w,h}; \lambda_{3};\dots; \lambda_{k})$}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The augmented geometric realization spectral sequence arising from the right Mayer--Vietoris complex of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)$ is the \emph{augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence} of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)$.
We write $E^{r}_{s,t}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]$ for the $(s,t)$-entry on the $r$-th page of this spectral sequence.
See Figure~\ref{right MV spectral sequence for SC} for the $E^{1}$-page of the augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence for $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)$.
head: environment

label: augmented right MVSS has trivial abutment
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{augmented right MVSS has trivial abutment}
The abutment of the augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)$ is trivial.
head: environment
labels: augmented right MVSS has trivial abutment

title: Proof
body_md:
Gonz\'{a}lez, Kahle, and the second author defined an augmented Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence \cite[Section 3.2]{gonzalez202615} that is equivalent to the geometric realization spectral sequence on the ordered analog of $MV_{\bullet}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big)$, so the resulting augmented spectral sequence has trivial abutment.
Moreover, this complex is a finite dimensional acyclic complex of free $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}[S_{n}]$-modules.
The $S_{n}$-action is free on this space, 
and the quotient is $MV_{\bullet}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big)$.
As such, the abutment of the augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)$ is trivial.
head: environment

label: connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost}
If $w,h\ge 2$, $n<wh$, and $0\le p\le \min\{h, n\}$, the square configuration space $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)$ is connected.
head: environment
labels: connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost

title: Proof
body_md:
We will show that the squares labeled $2$ can be moved to the top of the rightmost column in $R_{w,h}$.
Since all of the squares labeled $2$ are indistinguishable, this would prove that $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)$ is connected as the squares labeled $1$ can be freely arranged to any other configuration in the rest of the rectangle.

Given any configuration in $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)$, we may slide the squares labeled $2$ into the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$. 
If we are given a configuration in which the squares labeled $2$ are not the top $p$ squares in the rightmost column, then there is at least one square labeled $1$ in the top $p$ spots in this column. 
Since $n<wh$, we may slide the squares labeled $1$ not in the rightmost column so that the square immediately to the left of the topmost square labeled $1$ in the rightmost column is unoccupied.
Therefore, we may slide it out of the rightmost column, allowing us to slide the remaining squares in that column up one.
Repeating this process if necessary, we see that the squares labeled $2$ can be moved to the top of the rightmost column in $R_{w,h}$, proving that $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)$ is connected.

The cover $\{V_{l}\}_{l=1}^{p+1}$ of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};1;p)$ is cellular ensuring the well-definedness of the augmented slide spectral sequence.
This cellularity is obtained by subdividing the complex $DC_{n}(R_{w-1,h-1}; 1; p)$.

For more details see \cite[Section 2]{gonzalez202615}.

labels: E2 entry of slide spectral sequence h=2

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the zeroth row of the $\tilde{E}^{1}$-page of the augmented slide spectral sequence for $SC_{n}(R_{w,2}; 1;1)$.
It has three potentially non-trivial entries:
\begin{align*}
&\tilde{E}^{1}_{-1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2}; 1;1)\big]=H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2}; 1;1)\big),\\
&\tilde{E}^{1}_{0,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2}; 1;1)\big]\;\;=H_{0}(V_{1})\oplus H_{0}(V_{2}),\text{ and}\\
&\tilde{E}^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2}; 1;1)\big]=H_{0}(V_{1}\cap V_{2}).
\end{align*}

If $n<2$ or $n>2w$, then $SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)$ is empty; if $2\le n\le 2w-2$, then it is connected; and if $2w-2<n\le 2w$, then by Proposition~\ref{SCnRwh two components} it consists of two components.
By Proposition~\ref{Vl is SCp2}, we have that $V_{1}\simeq V_{2}\simeq SC_{n-2}(R_{w-1,2})$, which is connected for all $2\le n< 2w$ by Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost}; for $n=2w$ this space is a point.
Otherwise, it is empty.
Finally, by Proposition~\ref{intersection of V1 and V2 h=2}, we have that $V_{1}\cap V_{2}\simeq SC_{n-2}(R_{w-2,2})$.
Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost} implies this is connected if $2\le n\le 2w-2$; otherwise, it is empty.
It follows that the zeroth row of the first page of the augmented slide spectral sequence of $SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)$ is of one of the three forms depicted in Figure~\ref{slide spectral sequence for SC h=2 n s=1 p=1 simplfied}.

label: rung A prop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{rung A prop}
Let $w \ge 2$ and $2 \le n \le 2w$. Then
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big)
\cong \operatorname{coker}(\alpha),
\]
where $\alpha$ is the $\tilde{d}^{1}$-differential
\[
\tilde{d}^{1}:\tilde{E}^{1}_{1,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big]=H_{1}(V_{1} \cap V_{2}) \to H_{1}(V_{1}) \oplus H_{1}(V_{2})=\tilde{E}^{1}_{0,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big]
\]
of the augmented slide spectral sequence of $SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)$.
head: environment
name: Rung A: from $H_{1}\big(SC_{n-2}(R_{w-2,2})\big)$ to $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big)$

title: Proof
body_md:
The augmented slide spectral sequence is an augmented Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence, so its abutment is trivial.
Since only the negative first, zeroth, and first columns of the $\tilde{E}^{1}$-page are non-trivial, the map 
\[
\tilde{d}^{1} : \tilde{E}^{1}_{0,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big]=H_{1}(V_{1}) \oplus H_{1}(V_2) \to H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big)=\tilde{E}^{1}_{-1,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big]
\]
has kernel equal to the image of
$\alpha$ as the $\tilde{E}^{2}_{0,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big]$-entry must be $0$.
Moreover, this differential is surjective since the $\tilde{E}^{2}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big]$-entry vanishes by Proposition~\ref{ E2 entry of slide spectral sequence h=2}.
It follows that $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big)\cong \operatorname{coker}(\alpha)$.

label: rung B prop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{rung B prop}
Let $w \ge 2$ and $2 \le n \le 2w-2$. Then
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big)\cong \operatorname{coker}(\beta) \oplus \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},
\]
where $\beta$ is the $d^{1}$-differential
\[
d^{1}:E^{1}_{1,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big]=H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};2;1)\big) \to H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big)=E^{1}_{0,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big]
\]
of the augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence of $SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)$, and the free summand $\mathbb{Z}$ is the image of the $d^{2}$-differential in $E^{2}_{-1,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big]$.
head: environment
name: Rung B: from $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big)$ to $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big)$

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall $E^{1}_{s,t}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big] = H_{t}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};s+1;1)\big)$. 
Every nontrivial entry of the zeroth row is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
For $s = -1$ this is Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost}, for $s = 0$ it is Proposition~\ref{SCnRwh two components}, and for $s = 1$ it is
Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost} together with the equivalence
$SC_{n}(R_{w,2};2;1) \simeq SC_{n-3}(R_{w-2,2})$ obtained by sliding the squares labeled $2$ and $3$ to the far right of $R_{w,2}$ and noting that no square labeled $1$ can enter the two rightmost columns since the squares labeled $2$ occupy the entire height of the second rightmost column.
That same equivalence identifies $E^{1}_{1,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big]$ with $H_{1}\big(SC_{n-3}(R_{w-2,2})\big)$, the source of $\beta$.
 
By Proposition~\ref{augmented right MVSS has trivial abutment} the abutment of this spectral sequence is trivial.
Since only the negative first, zeroth, and first columns of the $E^{1}$-page of this spectral sequence can be nonzero, the image of
\[
d^{1}:E^{1}_{0,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big]=H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1;1)\big) \to H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big)=E^{1}_{-1,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big]
\]
is isomorphic to $\operatorname{coker}(\beta)$. 

By the definition of the
$d^{1}$-differentials on the zeroth row, $E^2_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big] \cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, and
triviality of the abutment forces
\[
d^2 : E^2_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big] \to E^2_{-1,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big] \cong H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2};1)\big)/\operatorname{coker}(\beta)
\]
to be an isomorphism.
Since the quotient is a free module, we get the desired splitting.

label: ladder remark
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{ladder remark}
Combining the three rungs gives a description of $H_1\big(SC_n(R_{w,2})\big)$ in terms of the homology of $SC_{n-2}(R_{w-1,2})$, $SC_{n-2}(R_{w-2,2})$, and $SC_{n-3}(R_{w-2,2})$. 
The first has the same value of $d$ as $SC_n(R_{w,2})$ and drives the induction on $w$. 
The second has $d$ two smaller, and the third has $d$ one smaller, driving the induction on $d$. 
In each of the cases below, the only work is to identify $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$.
This comes down to determining when there is enough unoccupied space in $R_{w,2}$ to identify two classes by sliding squares around.

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction on $w$.
In the case $w=2$, work of Alpert, Bauer, Kahle, MacPherson, and Spendlove \cite[Theorem 3.5]{alpert2023homology} proves that $SC_{2}(R_{2,2})$ is homotopy equivalent to the figure at the top right of Figure~\ref{Configsin2by2}.
It follows that $H_{1}\big(SC_{2}(R_{2,2})\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, and that $H_{1}\big(SC_{2}(R_{2,2})\big)$ is generated by a single even orbiting pair square class.

For the induction step, assume the lemma holds for all $w\le \omega$ for some $\omega\ge 2$.
We will show that the lemma holds for $w=\omega+1$ by using the three steps of our ladder, first using the inductive hypothesis to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1;1)\big)$, next using this to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1)\big)$, and finally using that to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2})\big)$.

\emph{Rung A:} By Proposition~\ref{intersection of V1 and V2 h=2} we have that $V_{1}\cap V_{2}\simeq SC_{2\omega-2}(R_{\omega-1,2})\simeq pt$, so $\alpha$ is the trivial map.
Since $V_{1}\simeq V_{2}\simeq SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1,2};2)\simeq SC_{2\omega-2}(R_{\omega,2})$ by Proposition~\ref{Vl is SCp2}, Proposition~\ref{rung A prop} implies that
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1;1)\big)\cong H_{1}(V_{1})\oplus H_{1}(V_{2})\cong H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-2}(R_{\omega, 2})\big)^{\oplus 2}.
\]
Moreover, the inductive hypothesis implies that  $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1;1)\big)$ is generated by the $\omega-1$ pairs of even orbiting pair square classes and the $\omega-2$ pairs of even orbiting triple square classes. 
Here each pair consists of the identical classes with the locations of the squares labeled $2$ and $3$ swapped; see Figure~\ref{GeneratorsH1SC6R4211}.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=.8\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=10cm]{GeneratorsH1SC6R4211.pdf}
\caption{The 6 generators of $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};1;1)\big)$.
Note that they come in pairs, where one element of each pair has the yellow square (the square labeled $2$) above the red square (the square labeled $3$), and the other below.
There are two locations for orbiting pair square class, but only one for the orbiting triple square class---in our bases we will never have such a class be as right as possible.}
\label{GeneratorsH1SC6R4211}
\end{figure}

\emph{Rung B:} 
We claim that $\beta$ is an injection. 
Observe that $SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\simeq SC_{2\omega-3}(R_{\omega-1,2})$.
This combined with Proposition~\ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-1} tells us that  
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\big)\cong H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-3}(R_{\omega-1,2})\big)\cong\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\omega-2},
\]
and this group is generated by $\omega-2$ orbiting triple square classes, one for each grid-preserving way of embedding $R_{2,2}$ into the $R_{\omega-1, 2}$ found on the left side of $R_{\omega+1,2}$.
The map $\beta$ sends orbiting triple square classes to the difference of a pair of orbiting triple square classes, which identifies the two classes in a pair of generators of $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1;1)\big)$ described in Rung A; see Figure~\ref{ClassinH1SC6R4221anditsimage}.
It follows from Proposition~\ref{rung B prop} that 
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1,2};1)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{3\omega-4} \oplus \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},
\]
where the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{3\omega-4}$ summand is generated by the $\omega-1$ pairs of even orbiting pair square classes and the $\omega-2$ even orbiting triple square classes. 
The $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ summand is the image of the $d^{2}$-differential, which is an even orbiting triple class with only the square labeled $2$ to its right by Proposition~\ref{spectral sequence d2 differential } as any $R_{2,2}$ embedded in $R_{\omega+1,2}$ in a grid respecting way contains at least three unit-squares.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=.8\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=6.25cm]{ClassinH1SC6R4221anditsimage.pdf}
\caption{At the top a generator of $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};2;1)\big)$.
At the bottom, the two classes in $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};1;1)\big)$, whose difference is the image of the above class under the $d^{1}$-differential.
See Figure~\ref{GeneratorsH1SC6R4211}.}
\label{ClassinH1SC6R4221anditsimage}
\end{figure}

\emph{Rung C:} We claim that $\operatorname{coker}(\gamma)$ is a direct summand of $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1)\big)$, and that it is isomorphic to $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-2}$.
By the inductive hypothesis, 
\[
E^{1}_{1,1}\big[SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2})\big]\cong H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\big)\cong H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-2}(R_{\omega, 2})\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-3}.
\]
This follows from the observation that $SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\simeq SC_{2\omega-2}(R_{\omega, 2})$ as the two squares labeled $2$ can be pushed to the far right of $R_{\omega+1, 2}$ and there is not enough space for any other square to enter the rightmost column.
Moreover, the inductive hypothesis tells us that this entry is generated by the $\omega-1$ even orbiting pair square classes and the $\omega-2$ even orbiting triple square classes. 
The map $\gamma$ sends the $\omega-2$ orbiting triple square classes to $0$ and an orbiting pair square class to the difference of a pair of the orbiting pair square class generators of $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1, 2});1\big)$ described in Rung B; see Figure~\ref{ClassesinH1SC6R422anditsimage}.
Therefore, its cokernel is isomorphic to $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-2}$. 
It follows from Proposition~\ref{rung C prop} that 
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega}(R_{\omega+1,2})\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-2} \oplus \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},
\]
where the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-2}$ summand is generated by the $\omega-1$ even orbiting pair square classes and the $\omega-1$ even orbiting triple square classes, and the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ summand is the image of the $d^{2}$-differential.
By Proposition~\ref{spectral sequence d2 differential }, this image corresponds to an even orbiting pair square class at the far right of $R_{\omega+1,2}$ as we can move the squares labeled $1$ about $R_{\omega+1,2}$ so that the grid squares immediately to the left of the squares labeled $2$ are unoccupied.
This completes the inductive step and hence the proof.

\centering
\captionsetup{width=.8\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=15cm]{ClassesinH1SC6R422anditsimage.pdf}
\caption{On the left, the orbiting triple square class in $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};2)\big)$ at the top, and the two classes in $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};1)\big)$ at the bottom whose difference is its image under the $d^{1}$-differential. Note these classes are homologous, so the $d^{1}$-differential sends this class to $0$.
On the right, an orbiting pair square class in $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};2)\big)$ at the top, and the two classes in $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};1)\big)$ at the bottom whose difference is its image under the $d^{1}$-differential.
Note these two classes are distinct generators of $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};1)\big)$, see Figure~\ref{GeneratorsH1SC6R421}, so the $d^{1}$-differential identifies them.}
\label{ClassesinH1SC6R422anditsimage}
\end{figure}

\centering
\captionsetup{width=.8\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=10cm]{GeneratorsH1SC6R421.pdf}
\caption{The $5$ generators of $H_{1}\big(SC_{6}(R_{4,2};1)\big)$ coming from the $d^{1}$-differential.
There are $2$ pairs of orbiting pair square classes and $1$ orbiting triple square class.
Here we have colored the square labeled $2$ red as we are implicitly using the identification $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};1)\simeq SC_{n}(R_{w,h};0;1)$.}
\label{GeneratorsH1SC6R421}
\end{figure}

body_md:
\label{first homology height 2 for 2w-3}
If $w\ge h=2$, then 
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{2w-3}(R_{w,2})\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2w-4},
\]
and it is generated by the $2w-4$ orbiting pair square classes corresponding to the possible ways of placing the $2w-5$ singleton squares on either side of the orbiting pair.

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction on $w$.
For $w=2$, Alpert, Bauer, Kahle, MacPherson, and Spendlove's work \cite[Theorem 3.5]{alpert2023homology} shows that $SC_{1}(R_{2,2})$ is homotopy equivalent to the figure at the top left of Figure~\ref{Configsin2by2}.
Therefore, $H_{1}\big(SC_{1}(R_{2,2})\big)=0$, proving the base case of our induction.

For the induction step, assume the lemma holds for all $w\le \omega$ for some $\omega\ge 2$.
We will show that the lemma holds for $w=\omega+1$ by using the three steps of our ladder, first using the inductive hypothesis to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1;1)\big)$, next using this to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1)\big)$, and finally using that to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1, 2})\big)$.

\emph{Rung A:} The map $\alpha$ is injective.
To see this, note that $V_{1}\cap V_{2}\simeq SC_{2\omega-3}(R_{\omega-1,2})$ by Proposition~\ref{intersection of V1 and V2 h=2}.
This fact and Proposition~\ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-1} prove that $H_{1}(V_{1}\cap V_{2})\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\omega-2}$; moreover, they prove that this group is generated by the $\omega-2$ orbiting triple square classes.
Next, note that the sets $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ are homotopy equivalent to $SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\simeq SC_{2\omega-3}(R_{\omega, 2})$ by Proposition~\ref{Vl is SCp2}, and it follows from the inductive hypothesis that $H_{1}(V_{1})\oplus H_{1}(V_{2})\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{4\omega-8}$, and that this group is generated by the $2\omega-4$ pairs of orbiting pair square classes corresponding to the $2\omega-4$ possible ways of placing the $2\omega-5$ singleton squares labeled $1$ on either side of the orbiting pair.
Here, each pair of classes is identical up to swapping the locations of the squares labeled $2$ and $3$; see the bottom of Figure~\ref{ClassinV1intersectV2anditsimage}.
By Proposition~\ref{orbiting triple classes are sums of squares} one can check that the image of an orbiting triple square class is a signed sum of four orbiting pair square classes as in Figure ~\ref{ClassinV1intersectV2anditsimage}.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=.8\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=13.75cm]{ClassinV1intersectV2anditsimage.pdf}
\caption{At the top, a class in $H_{1}(V_{1}\cap V_{2})$, and, at the bottom, the four generators of $H_{1}(V_{1})\oplus H_{1}(V_{2})$ whose signed sum makes up its image under the $d^{1}$-differential.
Namely, its image is the difference of the first and third classes with the second and fourth classes.
It follows that the first three of the classes at the bottom form a basis for $H_{1}\big(SC_{5}(R_{4,2};1;1)\big)$.
This relies on the fact that in $H_{1}\big(SC_{3}(R_{3,2})\big)$ an orbiting triple square class can be decomposed into the sum of two orbiting pair square classes via Proposition~\ref{orbiting triple classes are sums of squares}.
}
\label{ClassinV1intersectV2anditsimage}
\end{figure}
These four orbiting pair square classes come in pairs of two, and each class only appears in the image of the differential of one of the generators of $H_{1}(V_{1}\cap V_{2})$.
It follows that $\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{3\omega-6}$, so $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1;1)\big)$ has a basis consisting of $3\omega-6$ orbiting pair square classes by Proposition~\ref{rung A prop}.

\emph{Rung B:}  
Observe that $SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\simeq SC_{2\omega-4}(R_{\omega-1,2})$.
This combined with Lemma~\ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-2}, tells us that  
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\big)\cong H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-4}(R_{\omega-1,2})\big)\cong\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-5},
\]
and that it is generated by the $\omega-2$ even orbiting pair square classes and the $\omega-3$ even orbiting triple square classes. 

The map $\beta$ sends the orbiting triple square classes generating $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\big)$ to $0$ and the orbiting pair square classes generating $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\big)$ to the difference of the pair of orbiting pair square classes generating $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1,2};1;1)\big)$ described in Rung A, serving to identify them; see Figure~\ref{ClassinH1SC5R4221anditsimage}.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=.8\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=6.25cm]{ClassinH1SC5R4221anditsimage.pdf}
\caption{On the top, a class in $H_{1}\big(SC_{5}(R_{4,2};2;1)\big)$, and on the bottom, the two classes whose difference is its image in $H_{1}\big(SC_{5}(R_{4,2};1;1)\big)$; compare with Figure~\ref{ClassinV1intersectV2anditsimage}.
For $\omega>3$, one can see that an orbiting triple square class in $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-3}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\big)$ can be realized in such a way that the column immediately to the left of the yellow and red squares (the squares labeled $2$ and $3$, respectively) is unoccupied.
This proves that under the $d^{1}$-differential, such a class goes to $0$.
}
\label{ClassinH1SC5R4221anditsimage}
\end{figure}
This identification of orbiting pair square classes tells us that $\operatorname{coker}(\beta)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-4}$; moreover, it shows that we can take the $2\omega-4$ orbiting pair square classes corresponding to the $2\omega-4$ ways of placing the $2\omega-5$ singleton squares labeled $1$ on either side of the orbiting pair square class.
Therefore, Proposition~\ref{rung B prop} tells us that 
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1,2};1)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-4} \oplus \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},
\]
where the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-4}$ summand is generated by the $2\omega-4$ orbiting pair square classes with at least one singleton square labeled $1$ to the right of the orbiting pair.
The $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ summand is the image of the $d^{2}$-differential, which is an orbiting pair square class with only the square labeled $2$ to its right by Proposition~\ref{spectral sequence d2 differential } as we can ensure that the grid squares immediately to the left of the squares labeled $2$ are unoccupied.

\emph{Rung C:} We claim that $\gamma$ has trivial image, so $\operatorname{coker}(\gamma)=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-3}$ as $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-3}$ by Rung B.
To see this note that $H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-4}$ by the inductive hypothesis, as $SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\simeq SC_{2\omega-3}(R_{\omega, 2})$ by sliding the squares labeled $2$ to the far right of $R_{\omega+1,2}$.
Moreover, this group is generated by the $2\omega-4$ orbiting pair square classes.
The map $\gamma$ sends an orbiting pair square class to $0$ as the two classes whose difference constitutes its image are homologous via the relations produced in Rung B; see Figure~\ref{ClassinH1SC5R422anditsimage}. 
It follows from Proposition~\ref{rung C prop} that 
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{2\omega-1}(R_{\omega+1,2})\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-3} \oplus \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},
\]
where the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2\omega-3}$ summand is generated by $2\omega-3$ orbiting pair square classes in which at least one singleton square is to the right of the orbiting pair, and the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ summand is the image of the $d^{2}$-differential.
By Proposition~\ref{spectral sequence d2 differential }, this image corresponds to an orbiting pair square class at the far right of $R_{\omega+1,2}$, completing the inductive step and hence the proof.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=.8\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=6.25cm]{ClassinH1SC5R422anditsimage.pdf}
\caption{On the top, an orbiting pair square class in $H_{1}\big(SC_{5}(R_{4,2};2)\big)$; on the bottom, the two orbiting pair square classes in $H_{1}\big(SC_{5}(R_{4,2};1)\big)$ whose difference is its image under the $d^{1}$-differential. 
These classes are homologous via the relations produced in Rung B.}
\label{ClassinH1SC5R422anditsimage}
\end{figure}

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{first homology height 2 for n le 2w-4}
If $w\ge h=2$ and $1\le n\le 2w-3$, then 
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,2})\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-1},
\]
and it is generated by the $n-1$ orbiting pair square classes corresponding to the $n-1$ possible ways of placing the $n-2$ singleton squares on either side of the orbiting pair.
head: environment
labels: first homology height 2 for n le 2w-4

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction on $d=2w-n$.
Lemma~\ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-3} handles the base case.
Next, assume that the lemma holds for all $3\le d\le \delta$ for some $\delta\ge 3$; we will show that the lemma holds for $d=\delta+1$ by inducting on $w$.
In the first non-trivial case we have $w=\left\lceil\frac{\delta+2}{2}\right\rceil$, which must is at least $3$.
In either case, there are straight-line homotopies between $SC_{1}(R_{w,2})$ and $SC_{2}(R_{w,2})$ and the complexes on the top right and top left of Figure~\ref{Configsin2by2}, respectively.
From this picture it follows that $H_{1}\big(SC_{1}(R_{w,2})\big)=0$ and $H_{1}\big(SC_{2}(R_{w,2})\big)\cong\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, proving the base case of our induction on $w$.

Next, assume that the lemma holds for all $w\le \omega$, for some $\omega\ge 3$.
We will show that the lemma holds for $w=\omega+1$ and all $n=2\omega-\delta+1$ by using the three steps of our ladder, first using the inductive hypothesis to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1;1)\big)$, next using this to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1)\big)$, and finally using that to compute $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2})\big)$.

\emph{Rung A:} We claim that $\alpha$ is injective.
To see this, first note that $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$ are homotopy equivalent to $SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\simeq SC_{n-2}(R_{\omega, 2})$ by Proposition~\ref{Vl is SCp2}.
Therefore, $H_{1}(V_{1}) \oplus H_{1}(V_{2})\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{2n-6}$ by the inductive hypothesis. 
Furthermore, this direct sum is generated by $n-3$ pairs of orbiting pair square classes.
By Proposition~\ref{intersection of V1 and V2 h=2}, we have that $V_{1}\cap V_{2}\simeq SC_{n-2}(R_{\omega-1,2})$.
Therefore $H_{1}(V_{1}\cap V_{2})\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-3}$ by our inductive hypothesis on $d$ if $\delta+1>4$, i.e.,  $n<2\omega-2$, and by Lemma~\ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-2} if $\delta+1=4$, i.e., $n=2\omega-2$.
Additionally, if $n<2\omega-2$, this group is generated by $n-3$ orbiting pair square classes; if $n=2\omega-2$, it is generated by $\omega-2$ orbiting pair square classes and $\omega-3$ orbiting triple square classes.

Next, note that the image of an orbiting pair square class generating $H_{1}(V_{1}\cap V_{2})$ under $\alpha$ is the difference of a pair of generators of $H_{1}(V_{1})\oplus H_{1}(V_{2})$.
For $n=2\omega-2$, one can similarly check that each of the orbiting triple square classes gets sent of a pair of orbiting triple square classes in $H_{1}(V_{1})\oplus H_{1}(V_{2})$ that decomposes as a sum of orbiting pair square classes, one of which is already accounted for by the orbiting pair square classes coming from $H_{1}(V_{1}\cap V_{2})$, the other of which is not.
In either case, $\alpha$ is injective, so $\operatorname{coker}(\alpha)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-3}$, and $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1;1)\big)$ is generated by $n-3$ orbiting pair square classes corresponding to the ways of placing the $n-4$ singleton squares labeled $1$ on either side of the orbiting pair square class.

\emph{Rung B:} We claim that $\beta$ is the zero map.
To see this observe that $SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\simeq SC_{n-3}(R_{\omega-1,2})$.
This, combined with Lemma~\ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-3} if $\delta+1=4$ or the inductive hypothesis on $d$ if $\delta+1>4$, tells us that  
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1,2};2;1)\big)\cong H_{1}\big(SC_{n-3}(R_{\omega-1,2})\big)\cong\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-4},
\]
and that it is generated by the $n-4$ orbiting pair square classes corresponding to the ways of putting the $n-5$ singleton squares labeled $1$ on either side of the orbiting pair. 
There is enough space in $R_{\omega+1,2}$ to rearrange the squares to ensure that the two orbiting pair square classes $\beta$ produces are homologous; compare with Figure~\ref{ClassinH1SC5R4221anditsimage}.
It follows that $\beta$ is the zero map.

By Rung A we have that 
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1,2};1;1)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-3}.
\]
Since $\beta$ is the zero map, this is the cokernel of $\beta$.
Therefore, Proposition~\ref{rung B prop} tells us that 
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1,2};1)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-3} \oplus \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}},
\]
where the $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-3}$ summand is generated by the $n-3$ orbiting pair square classes with at least one singleton square labeled $1$ to the right of the orbiting pair.
The $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ summand is the image of the $d^{2}$-differential, which is an orbiting pair square class with only the square labeled $2$ to its right by Proposition~\ref{spectral sequence d2 differential }.

\emph{Rung C:}
We claim that $\gamma$ has trivial image, so $\operatorname{coker}(\gamma)=\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-2}$ as $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-2}$ by Rung B.
By the inductive hypothesis, $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-3}$ since $SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\simeq SC_{n-2}(R_{\omega, 2})$ by sliding the squares labeled $2$ to the far right of $R_{\omega+1,2}$.
Moreover, this entry is generated by the $n-3$ orbiting pair square classes.
We claim that every orbiting pair square class generating $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};2)\big)$ has trivial image in $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2};1)\big)$.
This follows from the fact that the two classes whose difference constitutes its image are homologous; see Figure~\ref{ClassinH1SC4R422anditsimage}.
It follows from Proposition~\ref{rung C prop} that $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{\omega+1, 2})\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{n-1}$.
Moreover, that proposition and Proposition~\ref{spectral sequence d2 differential } prove that this group is generated by the $n-1$ orbiting pair square classes corresponding to the ways of placing the $n-2$ singleton squares on either side of the orbiting pair.
This completes the inductive step on $w$, hence the inductive step on $d$ and the proof of the lemma.
\begin{figure}[h]
\centering
\captionsetup{width=.8\linewidth}
\includegraphics[width=6.25cm]{ClassinH1SC4R422anditsimage.pdf}
\caption{On the top, an orbiting pair square class in $H_{1}\big(SC_{4}(R_{4,2};2)\big)$; on the bottom, the two orbiting pair square classes in $H_{1}\big(SC_{4}(R_{4,2};1)\big)$ whose difference is its image under the $d^{1}$-differential. 
The excess of unoccupied space in $R_{4,2}$ ensures that these classes are homologous.}
\label{ClassinH1SC4R422anditsimage}
\end{figure}

body_md:
Proposition~\ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-1} proves the theorem in the case $n=2w-1$.
Lemmas~\ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-2}, \ref{first homology height 2 for 2w-3}, and \ref{first homology height 2 for n le 2w-4} prove the theorem for $n=2w-2$, $n=2w-3$, and $1\le n\le 2w-4$, respectively.

label: connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost
title: Proposition
head: environment
labels: connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost

title: Proof
body_md:
Throughout the proof, we use the fact that we can slide the squares labeled $3$ into the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$ and the squares labeled $2$ into the second rightmost column.
First, we treat the three connected cases, then we treat the disconnected ones.

\emph{Case (i):} If $s+p+1>h$, then only squares labeled $3$ can be in the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$.
If we forget that column, we get a configuration in $SC_{n-p}(R_{w-1, h}; s+1)$.
This configuration space is connected by Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost}, so $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};s+1; p)$ is as well.

\emph{Case (ii):} If $s+p+1\le h$ and $n\le (w-1)h+p-1$, and the $s+1$ squares labeled $2$ are not in the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$, then we may slide the $p$ squares labeled $3$ up and down so that the grid squares to the right of the squares labeled $2$ are unoccupied, allowing us to move them into the rightmost column. 
Therefore, we may assume that all squares labeled $2$ or $3$ are in the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$.
Treating all squares labeled $2$ or $3$ as rightmost, Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost} ensures that they can be moved into the first $s+p+1$ entries in the rightmost column.

We show that the squares labeled $2$ can be moved to the top of this column.
Since $n\le (w-1)h+p-1$, if there is a square labeled $3$ above a square labeled $2$, we may slide the squares labeled $1$ about so that the grid squares immediately to the left of the squares labeled $2$ are unoccupied and such that the square one to the left and one up from the highest square labeled $2$ that is below a square labeled $3$ is unoccupied. 
Moreover, we can do this while keeping the squares labeled $1$ out of the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$.
Therefore, we can slide the squares labeled $2$ into the second rightmost column, and the highest square labeled $2$ that was below a square labeled $3$ up one, while sliding the square labeled $3$ that was above this square down one.
Sliding the squares labeled $2$ back into the rightmost column, we see that at least one of them could be moved up.
Repeating this process if necessary, all the squares labeled $2$ can be put directly above all of the squares labeled $3$ in the rightmost column, showing that this configuration space is connected.

\emph{Case (iii):} If $s+p+1<h$ and $n=(w-1)h+p$, and the $s+1$ squares labeled $2$ are not in the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$, then we may slide the $p$ squares labeled $3$ up and down so that the grid squares to the right of the squares labeled $2$ are unoccupied, allowing us to move them into the rightmost column. 
Therefore, we may assume that all squares labeled $2$ or $3$ are in the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$.
Treating all squares labeled $2$ or $3$ as rightmost, Proposition 
\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost} allows us to assume that the squares labeled $2$ and $3$ are at the top of this column.

We prove that the squares can be slid around the rectangle so that the squares labeled $2$ are above all the squares labeled $3$.
If there is a square labeled $3$ directly above a square labeled $2$, note that since $n=(w-1)h+p$, we can slide the squares labeled $1$ about the left part of $R_{w,h}$ so that the squares immediately to the left of the squares labeled $2$ are unoccupied.
Furthermore, since $n\le wh-3$, $s+1\le 3$, and $s+p+1<h$, after pushing the squares labeled $3$ that are below all the squares labeled $2$ to the bottom of the rightmost column, we can slide the lowest square labeled $3$ that is immediately above a square labeled $2$ down so that it is now below it.
Sliding the squares labeled $2$ back to the right, we see that they can be moved up in the rightmost column.
Repeating this process if necessary, we see that the squares labeled $2$ can be put at the top of the rightmost column with the squares labeled $3$ below them, showing that this configuration space is connected.
 
\emph{The disconnected cases:} It remains to show that outside of these cases $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; s+1;p)$ has $\binom{s+p+1}{p}$ components.
We do this by dividing this situation into two cases:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(iv)] $s+p+1=h$ and $n\ge (w-1)h+p$;

    \item [(v)] $s+p+1<h$ and $n\ge (w-1)h+p+1$.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Case (iv):} If $s+p+1=h$ and $n\ge (w-1)h+p$, then there is no room to slide the squares labeled $2$ around the rectangle.
If $n>(w-1)h+p$, the squares labeled $2$ are constrained to the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$, and if $n=(w-1)h+p$, then they can be slid one to the right but not up or down.
As $s+p+1=h$, the $p$ squares labeled $3$ cannot be rearranged while the squares labeled $2$ are in the second rightmost column, so no new interweaving of the squares labeled $2$ and $3$ can be produced.
Since the space would be connected if we relabeled all of the squares labeled $3$ to $2$, there is one component for each way of placing the $s+1$ squares labeled $2$ between the $p$ squares labeled $3$, i.e., there are $\binom{s+p+1}{p}$ components.

\emph{Case (v):} If $s+p+1<h$ and $n\ge (w-1)h+p+1$, then the squares labeled $2$ must be in the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$.
Since the space would be connected if we relabeled all of the squares labeled $3$ to $2$, we see that there is one component for each way of placing the $s+1$ squares labeled $2$ between the $p$ squares labeled $3$, so there are $\binom{s+p+1}{p}$ components.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $n=p+2$, then $n-p-1=1\neq (w-1)h$.
It follows from Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost} that $E^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]=H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 2;p)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$.
Similarly, one can use Propositions~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost} and \ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost} to see that $E^{1}_{0,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]=H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $E^{1}_{-1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]=H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, whereas $E^{1}_{2,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]=H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 3;p)\big)=0$ as $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 3;p)$ is empty.
It follows from the definition of the differentials of the augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence that $E^{2}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$. 

If $n\neq p+2$, then Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost} tells us there are two possibilities to consider: $E^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ and $E^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\binom{p+2}{p}}$.
In the first case, one can note that Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost} implies that $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};1;p)$ is also connected, so the kernel of 
\[
d^{1}:E^{1}_{1,0}=H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};2;p)\big)\to H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};1;p)\big)=E^{1}_{0,0}
\]
is all of $E^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]$.
This follows from the observation that relabeling either square labeled $2$ to $1$ gives homologous classes since $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};1;p)$ is connected.
Since $n\le wh-3$, we have that $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};2;p)$ is nonempty, and the image of 
\[
d^{1}:E^{1}_{2,0}=H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};3;p)\big)\to H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};2;p)\big)= E^{1}_{1,0}
\]
is all of $E^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]$.
This follows from the fact that all three classes coming from relabeling a square labeled $2$ to $1$ in any representative of the natural basis for $H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 3;p)\big)$ are homologous, so since two of them cancel, the third remains. 
Therefore $E^{2}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]\cong 0$.

If $E^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]=H_{0}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};2;p)\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\binom{p+2}{p}}$, then $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};3;p)$ is non-empty as $n\le wh-3$.
Moreover, Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost} implies $E^{1}_{2,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\binom{p+3}{p}}$.
Further, Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost} implies $E^{1}_{0,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{p+1}$.
To see this note that the only other possibility is that $E^{1}_{0,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, which is only possible if $n=wh-2$ given $E^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}^{\binom{p+2}{p}}$.
In this case, the $E^{1}_{0,0}$-, $E^{1}_{1,0}$-, and $E^{1}_{2,0}$-entries of the augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence correspond to the $2$-skeleton of a simplicial complex, whose $(q-1)$-simplices correspond to ways of shuffling $q$ elements into a set of $p$ elements.
This complex has trivial first homology, so $E^{2}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p)\big]\cong0$.

body_md:
We begin by noting that in $V_{l_{i}}$, if the square labeled $2$ is not in the same column of $R_{w,h}$ as the squares labeled $3$, then the highest row it can fully be in is the $l_{i}$-th row of $R_{w,h}$ when counting from the top.
This follows from the fact that there must be enough space to slide it directly to the right so that $l_{i}-1$ squares labeled $3$ can fit above it.
Similarly, the lowest row it can be fully contained in is the $(h-p-1+l_{i})$-th row from the top, as there must be space for $p+1-l_{i}$ squares beneath it when slid to the right.
Moreover, the square labeled $2$ can be anywhere between these rows.
It follows that in $V$, the highest this square labeled $2$ can be is the $l_{s}$-th row, and the lowest it can be is the $(h-p-1+l_{0})$-th row.
Thus, this intersection is empty if $l_{s}-l_{0}>h-p-1$.

Next, note that since $s\ge 1$, we may assume that in $V$ the square labeled $2$ is in the second rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$.
This follows from the observation that in $V$ the square labeled $2$ cannot be in the same column as the squares labeled $3$ and the fact that we can push the squares labeled $3$ to the far right of $R_{w,h}$ and ignore them, and then push the square labeled $2$ into the second rightmost column.

\emph{Case 1.)} If $n<(w-1)h+p$, then there is at least one unoccupied square in the $R_{w-1,h}$ found on the left side of $R_{w,h}$.
Thus, the square labeled $2$ can be slid up or down between the rows proving that $V$ is connected.

\emph{Case 2.)} If $n=(w-1)h+p$, then there are $(w-1)h$ squares labeled $1$ or $2$ in the $R_{w-1,h}$ found on the left side of $R_{w,h}$.
Therefore these squares cannot move.
It follows that $V$ has $h-p+l_{0}-l_{s}$ components, one for each row between the $l_{s}$-th and the $(h-p-1+l_{0})$-th row inclusive. 

\emph{Case 3.)} If $n>(w-1)h+p$, then the square labeled $2$ must be in the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$.
Since it is in different positions relative to the squares labeled $3$ in $V_{l_{0}}$ and $ V_{l_{s}}$, the intersection is empty.

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{Vl is SCp2}, in the augmented slide spectral sequence of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h};1;p)$ the $\tilde{d}^{1}$-differential from $\tilde{E}^{1}_{0,1}$ to $\tilde{E}^{1}_{-1,1}$ is a map
\[
H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p+1)\big)^{\oplus(p+1)}\to H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};1;p)\big).
\]
The only other potentially non-trivial entry mapping into $\tilde{E}^{r}_{-1,1}$ under the $\tilde{d}^{r}$-differential is the $\tilde{E}^{r}_{1,0}$-entry.
Since the abutment of this spectral sequence is trivial, it suffices to determine that entry.

If $n=(w-1)h+p$ and $h\ge 4$, note that the sets $V_{l}$ used to define the augmented slide spectral sequence are connected by Propositions~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces one rightmost} and~\ref{Vl is SCp2}.
Additionally, if $l_{s}-l_{0}\le h-p-1$, the intersections $V_{l_{0}}\cap\cdots\cap V_{l_{s}}$ are nonempty via Proposition~\ref{connected intersection of Vs n-p-1 < (w-1)h}, and this intersection has $h-p+l_{0}-l_{s}$ components, one for each possible location of the square labeled $2$ in the second rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$.
Noting that it suffices to consider $l_{s}-l_{0}=1$, it follows that $\tilde{E}^{2}_{s,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1; p)\big]$ is the $s$-th homology group of the complex that arises from taking $h-p-1$ copies of the nerve complex $N(\mathcal{V})$ described in the $n<(w-1)h+p$ case of Proposition~\ref{nerve complex is contractible} and for each $i$, identifying all the zero cells labeled by $V_{l_{i}}$.
By the proof of Proposition~\ref{nerve complex is contractible}, this is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of circles corresponding to pairs $(l, l+1)$, where for each pair there are $h-p-2$ loops.
By standard spectral sequence techniques, one can check that the images of these loops  under the $\tilde{d}^{2}$-differential are the exotic classes depicted Figure~\ref{exotic class}.
Since this space is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of circles and the $\tilde{E}^{r}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1; p)\big]$-entry must vanish on subsequent pages, this gives a free $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-module of rank $p(h-p-2)$ generated by exotic classes.
As this module is free, $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)$ 
is canonically a direct sum of a quotient of $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p+1)\big)^{\oplus(p+1)}$ and the free $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-module generated by $p(h-p-2)$ exotic classes.

If $n\neq (w-1)h+p$ or $h<4$, then Proposition~\ref{nerve complex is contractible} proves that $\tilde{E}^{2}_{s,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1; p)\big]=0$.
Therefore, $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)$ is canonically a quotient of $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h};p+1)\big)^{\oplus(p+1)}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence for $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)$.
There are two cases we consider: $n=p+2$ and $n\neq p+2$.

If $n=p+2$, then $n-p-1=1\neq (w-1)h$.
It follows that $E^{1}_{0,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]=H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)=0$ as $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)$ is a quotient of $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p+1)\big)^{\oplus(p+1)}=0$ by Proposition~\ref{H1 SC(1p1)}.
This follows from the fact that there is a straight-line homotopy $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p+1)\simeq SC_{1}(R_{w-1,h})\simeq pt$ that pushes the squares labeled $2$ into the rightmost column of $R_{w,h}$ and the square labeled $1$ out of that column.
Therefore, $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big)$ is the image of $E^{2}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]$ under the $d^{2}$-differential.
This entry is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ as by Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost}, the $E^{1}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]$-entry is $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, the $d^{1}$-differential from this entry is $0$ as $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)$ is connected by Proposition~\ref{connected unordered square configuration spaces two rightmost}, and the $E^{1}_{2,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]$-entry is $0$.
By Proposition~\ref{spectral sequence d2 differential }, the image of this differential is an orbiting pair square class, so $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big)$ is generated by an orbiting pair square class.


If $n\neq p+2$, a similar argument works, but, in this case, $E^{2}_{1,0}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]=0$ by Proposition~\ref{E201 entry of augmeneted right Mayer Vietoris ss}.
It follows that the $d^{1}$-differential from $E^{1}_{0,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]=H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)$ to $E^{1}_{-1,1}\big[SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big]=H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big)$ is surjective as the augmented right Mayer--Vietoris spectral sequence of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)$ has trivial abutment by Proposition~\ref{augmented right MVSS has trivial abutment}.
Therefore, $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big)$ is a quotient of $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)$.
Note $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)$ is a direct sum of a quotient of $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p+1)\big)^{\oplus(p+1)}$ and a free summand spanned by exotic classes by Proposition~\ref{H1 SC(1p1)}.
As $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p+1)\big)$ is generated by orbiting pair square classes and exotic classes by assumption, $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; 1;p)\big)$, hence $H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h}; p)\big)$, must be as well.

H_{1}\big(SC_{n}(R_{w,h})\big)\to H_{1}\big(C_{n}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})\big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}
\]
sends an orbiting pair square class to a generator, this map is a surjection, implying that the inclusion of $SC_{n}(R_{w,h})$ into $C_{n}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})$ induces an isomorphism on first homology for $w,h\ge 3$ and $n\le wh-3$.

title: Lemma

\label{higher differentials}
Let $n=m2^{s}$, where $m$ is odd, and let $A_{n}$ be the generator of $H_{0}\Big(Arc_{n-1}\big(C_{n}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})\big);\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Big)$, the $(n-1,0)$-entry of the first page of the augmented arc resolution spectral sequence of $C_{n}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})$ with $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-coefficients.
Then
\[
d^{q}(A_{n})=0\qquad\text{for}\quad q<2^{s},
\]
and
\[
d^{2^{s}}(A_{n})=[P_{s}\otimes A_{(m-1)2^{s}}].
\]
where the square bracket denotes the class taken in homology.

Let $M$ be the interior of a (not necessarily compact) smooth manifold $\overline{M}$ with nonempty boundary $\partial M$.
Fix an embedding $\gamma:[0,1]\to \partial M$.
Let
\[
\text{Arc}_{p}\big(F_{n}(M)\big)\subset F_{n}(M)\times \text{Emb}\big(\sqcup_{p+1}[0,1], \overline{M}\big)
\]
be the subspace of points and arcs $(x_{1}, \dots, x_{n}; \alpha_{0},\dots, \alpha_{p})$ satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\alpha_{i}(0)\in \gamma\big([0,1]\big)$,
    
    \item $\alpha_{i}(1)\in \{x_{1},\dots, x_{n}\}$,
    
    \item $\alpha_{i}(t)\notin \partial M\cup \{x_{1}, \dots, x_{n}\}$ for $t\in (0,1)$, and

    \item $\gamma^{-1}\big(\alpha_{i}(0)\big)>\gamma^{-1}\big(\alpha_{j}(0)\big)$ whenever $i>j$.
\end{itemize}
Let $\text{Arc}_{p}\big(C_{n}(M)\big)$ denote the quotient of $\text{Arc}_{p}\big(F_{n}(M)\big)$ by the natural $S_{n}$-action.

title: Proof
body_md:
We define our arc resolution spectral sequence by noting that $C_{n}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})$ is homotopy equivalent to $C_{n}(R_{n,n})$ and defining the image of $\gamma$ to be the right side of the rectangle parameterized downwards.
Next, note that $Arc_{p}\big(C_{n}(R_{n,n})\big)$ is equivalent to the subspace in which all of the arcs are trivial, i.e., the points attached to the arcs lie on the right side of $R_{w,h}$.
Given this equivalence, one can check that the homotopy equivalence of \cite[Theorem 18]{plachta2021configuration} induces a homotopy equivalence $Arc_{p}\big(C_{n}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})\big)\simeq MV_{p}\big(SC_{n}(R_{n,n})\big)$.
Moreover, this sequence of homotopies commutes with the face maps.
Since the semisimplicial spaces $Arc_{\bullet}\big(C_{n}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})\big)$ and $ MV_{\bullet}\big(SC_{n}(R_{n,n})\big)$ are homotopy equivalent, the resulting spectral sequences are isomorphic.

label: Leibniz rule for arc resolution
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Leibniz rule for arc resolution}
The maps $e_{p,p'}$ induce maps
\[
t^{r}:E^{r}_{p,q}(m)\otimes E^{r}_{p',q'}(n)\to E^{r}_{p+p'+1, q+q'}(m+n).
\]
These maps satisfy the following Leibniz rule with respect to the differentials:
if $X\in E^{r}_{p,q}(m)$ and $Y\in E^{r}_{p',q'}(n)$, then
\[
d^{r}\big(t^{r}(X\otimes Y)\big)=t^{r}\big(d^{r}(X)\otimes Y\big)+(-1)^{p+q}t^{r}\big(X\otimes d^{r}(Y)\big).
\]

label: derivation prop
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{derivation prop}
For every \(s\ge 0\), $Z_{2^{s}}$ is a derivation over $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, namely
\[
Z_{2^{s}}(X\otimes Y) = Z_{2^{r}}(X)\otimes Y + X\otimes Z_{2^{s}}(Y),
\]
whenever the relevant zigzags are defined.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The zigzag $Z$ is a derivation on chains, so iterating the Leibniz rule gives
\[
Z_{2^{s}}(X\otimes Y) = \sum_{k=0}^{2^{s}} \binom{2^{s}}{k} Z_{k}(X)\otimes Z_{(2^{s}-k)}(Y).
\]

For $1\le k\le 2^{s}-1$, the coefficient $\binom{2^{s}}{k}$ is even. 
Indeed, in characteristic $2$, we have $(a+b)^{2^{s}}=a^{2^{s}}+b^{2^{s}}$.
Therefore, all intermediate terms vanish over $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, leaving
\[
Z_{2^{s}}(X\otimes Y) = Z_{2^{s}}(X)\otimes Y + X\otimes Z_{2^{s}}(Y)
\]
as desired.

label: zigzag of An
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{zigzag of An}
If $n=l2^{s+1}$, then 
\[
Z_{2^{s}}(A_{n})=\sum_{k=0}^{l-1} A_{k2^{s+1}} \otimes M_{s+1} \otimes A_{(l-k-1)2^{s+1}}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction on $s$.
For $s=0$, we have that $n=2l$, and 
\[
Z_{0}(A_{n})=d_{h}(A_{n})=\sum_{j=0}^{2l-1}A_{j}\otimes P_{0}\otimes A_{2l-j-1}.
\]
As we are working with $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-coefficients we can pair of the form $A_{2k}\otimes P_{0}\otimes A_{1}\otimes A_{2l-2k-2}$ and  $A_{2k}\otimes A_{1}\otimes P_{0} \otimes A_{2l-2k-2}$.
Such a pair admits a lift $\psi(P_{0}, A_{0})=M_{1}$ under $d^{-1}_{v}$, so
\[
Z_{1}(A_{n})=Z(A_{n})=\sum_{k=0}^{l-1}A_{2k}\otimes M_{1}\otimes A_{2(l-k-1)},
\]
proving the statement for $s=0$.

Now suppose the proposition holds for all $s\le \sigma$.
We wish to show that it holds for $s=\sigma+1$.
Given $n=l2^{\sigma+1}$, we first apply $Z_{2^{\sigma-1}}$.
By the inductive hypothesis,
\[
Z_{2^{\sigma-1}}(A_{n})=\sum^{2l-1}_{j=0}A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes M_{\sigma}\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}.
\]
Instead of computing $Z_{2^{\sigma-1}}(A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes M_{\sigma}\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}})$ to get $Z_{2^{\sigma}}(A_{n})$, which would lead to an ill-defined term, we perform $2^{\sigma-1}-1$ zigzags on $M_{\sigma}$ and compute the final zigzag separately to get $Z_{2^{\sigma}}(A_{n})$.
Successively applying $Z_{2^{\sigma-2}}, Z_{2^{\sigma-3}},\dots, Z_{2^{0}}$ to the internal arc block of $M_{\sigma}$, we see that at each stage the size of this block is reduced by a factor of $2$, and at the end of this process exactly one arc remains; see Figure~\ref{SuccessiveZs}.
\begin{figure}[H]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=8.75cm]{SuccessiveZs.pdf}
    \caption{Successive applications of $Z_{2}$ and $Z_{1}$ on $M_{3}$.}
    \label{SuccessiveZs}
\end{figure}.


Expanding these zigzags by Proposition~\ref{derivation prop}, we see that
\begin{multline*}
Z_{2^{\sigma-1}-1}(A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes M_{\sigma}\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}})\\
=\sum_{a+b+c=2^{\sigma-1}-1}\binom{2^{\sigma-1}-1}{a,b,c}Z_{a}(A_{j2^{\sigma}})\otimes Z_{b}(M_{\sigma})\otimes Z_{c}(A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}})\\
=\sum_{\substack{a+b+c=2^{\sigma-1}-1\\b\neq 2^{\sigma-1}-1}}\binom{2^{\sigma-1}-1}{a,b,c}Z_{a}(A_{j2^{\sigma}})\otimes Z_{b}(M_{\sigma})\otimes Z_{c}(A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}})\\
+A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes Z_{2^{\sigma-1}-1}(M_{\sigma})\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}.
\end{multline*}

To determine $Z_{1}$ of $A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes Z_{2^{\sigma-1}-1}(M_{\sigma})\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}$, we first apply $d_{h}$, and then take a lift along $d_{v}^{-1}$.
\begin{align*}
d_{h}\big(A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes Z_{2^{\sigma-1}-1}(M_{\sigma})\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}\big)&=d_{h}(A_{j2^{\sigma}})\otimes Z_{2^{\sigma-1}-1}(M_{\sigma})\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}\\
&+A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes d_{h}\big(Z_{2^{\sigma-1}-1}(M_{\sigma})\big)\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}\\
&+A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes Z_{2^{\sigma-1}-1}(M_{\sigma})\otimes d_{h}(A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}).
\end{align*}
The first and third terms have well-defined lifts, but the middle term does not.
Setting $Q_{j}=A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes Z^{\sigma-1}(M_{\sigma})\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}$, we pair off $Q_{2k}$ and $Q_{2k+1}$, and return to them later.

Computing $Z_{1}$ of the terms in the sum, we see that by the trinomial theorem and the fact that we are working with $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-coefficients, this sum reduces to 
\[
Z_{2^{\sigma-1}}(A_{j2^{\sigma}})\otimes M_{\sigma}\otimes A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}+A_{j2^{\sigma}}\otimes M_{\sigma}\otimes Z_{2^{\sigma-1}}(A_{(2l-j-1)2^{\sigma}}).
\]
Taking the sum of these terms as $j$ ranges from $0$ to $2l-1$, we get $0$ by the inductive hypothesis as we can pair off terms.
It follows that
\[
Z_{2^{\sigma}}(A_{n})=\sum^{l-1}_{k=0}d^{-1}_{h}(Q_{2k}+Q_{2k+1}).
\]
Each pair $Q_{2k}+Q_{2k+1}$ lifts to the pure twist $P_{\sigma}$ together with the adjacent block of $2^{\sigma}$ arcs, i.e., the $(\sigma+1)$-mixed twist $M_{\sigma+1}$, sandwiched between $A_{k2^{\sigma+1}}$ and $A_{(l-k-1)2^{\sigma+1}}$, yielding
\[
Z_{2^{\sigma}}(A_{n})=\sum^{l-1}_{k=0}A_{k2^{\sigma+1}}\otimes M_{\sigma+1}\otimes A_{(l-k-1)2^{\sigma+1}},
\]
as desired.

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction on $s$.

If $s=0$, then $n=m$, and the chain $A_{n}$ consists of an odd number of arcs.
Applying the horizontal differential to $A$ yields $n$ homologous classes in $H_{0}\Big(Arc_{n-2}\big(C_{n}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})\big);\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Big)$, each of which corresponds to a single unattached point and $n-1=m-1$ arcs, i.e., $\left[P_{0}\otimes A_{m-1}\right]$.
Since we are working with $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$-coefficients, and $n=m$ is odd, we see that the image of this class under the $d^{1}$-differential is $\left[P_{0}\otimes A_{m-1}\right]$, as desired.

Next, suppose that the lemma holds for all $n=m2^{s}$, where $s\le \sigma$, for some non-negative integer $\sigma$.
We will we show that it holds for all $n$ of the form $m2^{\sigma+1}$.
Consider $A_{n}$, where $n=m2^{\sigma+1}$.
We have that
\[
d^{2^{\sigma+1}}(A_{n})=d_{h}\big(Z_{2^{\sigma+1}-1}(A_{n})\big)=d_{h}\Big(Z_{2^{\sigma}-1}\big(Z_{2^{\sigma}}(A_{n})\big)\Big)
\]
Since $2^{\sigma+1}$ divides the number of arcs, Proposition~\ref{zigzag of An} yields
\[
Z_{2^{\sigma}}(A_{n})=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}A_{j2^{\sigma+1}}\otimes M_{\sigma+1}\otimes A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}}.
\]
Applying $Z_{2^{\sigma}-1}$ to the summands, Proposition~\ref{derivation prop} yields  
\begin{multline*}
Z_{2^{\sigma}-1}(A_{j2^{\sigma+1}}\otimes M_{\sigma+1}\otimes A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}})\\
=\sum_{a+b+c=2^{\sigma}-1}\binom{2^{\sigma}-1}{a,b,c}Z_{a}(A_{j2^{\sigma+1}})\otimes Z_{b}(M_{\sigma+1})\otimes Z_{c}(A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}}),
\end{multline*}
so
\[
Z_{2^{\sigma+1}-1}(A_{n})=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\sum_{a+b+c=2^{\sigma}-1}\binom{2^{\sigma}-1}{a,b,c}Z_{a}(A_{j2^{\sigma+1}})\otimes Z_{b}(M_{\sigma+1})\otimes Z_{c}(A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}}).
\]

Applying $d_{h}$ to this sum, we see that since $a$ and $c$ are at most $2^{\sigma}-1$, and $j2^{\sigma+1}$ and $(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}$ are divisible by $2^{\sigma+1}$, the inductive hypothesis implies  implies that $d_{h}\big(Z_{a}(A_{j2^{\sigma+1}})\big)$ and $d_{h}\big(Z_{c}(A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}})\big)$ are $0$.
Therefore,
\[
d^{2^{\sigma+1}}(A_{n})=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\sum_{a+b+c=2^{\sigma}-1}\binom{2^{\sigma}-1}{a,b,c}Z_{a}\left(A_{j2^{\sigma+1}}\right)\otimes d_{h}\big(Z_{b}(M_{\sigma+1})\big)\otimes Z_{c}\left(A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}}\right).
\]

Next, noting that $M_{\sigma+1}=\psi\big(P_{\sigma}, A_{2^{\sigma}}\big)$, we see that if $b<2^{\sigma}-1$, then by the inductive hypothesis, $A_{2^{\sigma}}$ supports another zigzag, so $d_{h}\big(Z_{b}(M_{\sigma+1})\big)$ is trivial in homology.
Therefore,
\[
d^{2^{\sigma+1}}(A_{n})=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}A_{j2^{\sigma+1}}\otimes d_{h}\big(Z_{2^{\sigma}-1}(M_{\sigma+1})\big)\otimes A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}}.
\]
Since $Z_{2^{\sigma}-1}=Z_{1}\circ\cdots\circ Z_{2^{\sigma-1}}$; see Figure~\ref{SuccessiveZs}, we see that there is exactly one arc in $\big(Z_{2^{\sigma}-1}(M_{\sigma+1})\big)$.
Apply $d_{h}$, we see that we obtain a $(\sigma+1)$-pure twist $P_{\sigma+1}$.
It follows that
\[
d^{2^{\sigma+1}}(A_{n})=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\left[A_{j2^{\sigma+1}}\otimes P_{\sigma+1}\otimes A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}}\right]=\left[A_{j2^{\sigma+1}}\otimes P_{\sigma+1}\otimes A_{(m-j-1)2^{\sigma+1}}\right].
\]
Here, the latter equality comes from the observations that the $m$ summands represent the same class, $m$ is odd, and we are working with $\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$ coefficients.

Lastly, we note that since $A_{n}$ generates $H_{0}\Big(Arc_{n-1}\big(C_{n}\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^{2})\big);\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}\Big)\cong \ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}/2\ensuremath{\mathbb{Z}}$, it follows that $d^{q}(A_{n})=0$ for $q<2^{\sigma+1}$, completing the inductive step and the proof.
